title: Digging the Trench
subtitle: Salman's Stratagem, Hunger, Unity, and Signs of Victory
summary: The digging of the trench in the classical account, the hunger and the poem in Bukhari, Jabir's meal in Bukhari 4101 and 4102, and a separate Musnad report of three strikes whose edition number is not 18703.

sections.text: In the bitter winter of the fifth year of the Hijrah (Shawwal 5 AH), the entire Muslim population of Madinah mobilized to execute Salman's engineering stratagem. The task was monumental: excavating a deep, broad ditch across the northern gap of the city, spanning from the crags of Mount Sal' to the edge of the volcanic lava plain of Harrat al-Wabrah—a distance of several kilometers. The trench had to be wide enough to prevent an Arabian warhorse from clearing it in a single leap, and deep enough that any armed rider descending into it could not scale the opposite embankment.

The classical sirah describes the division of the work and gives a Muslim strength of about three thousand, with parties measured by cubits. Those figures are not in the Bukhari reports of the digging. The sirah also reports that the Muhajirun and the Ansar each wanted Salman with them, and that the Prophet said Salman was one of them, of the people of the household. That saying is not given a Hadith number here.

The physical toil was grueling. Madinah was experiencing an acute drought and famine; food supplies were scarce, and bitter north winds chilled the diggers to the bone. The Prophet ﷺ worked side by side with his companions, swinging pickaxes, hauling baskets of earth upon his shoulders, and raising his voice in rhythmic verses to sustain their spirits. Al-Bara' ibn Azib reported seeing the Messenger of Allah ﷺ carrying earth until the dust obscured the whiteness of his chest, chanting the poetry of Ibn Rawahah:

اللَّهُمَّ لَوْلَا أَنْتَ مَا اهْتَدَيْنَا * وَلَا تَصَدَّقْنَا وَلَا صَلَّيْنَا
فَأَنْزِلَنْ سَكِينَةً عَلَيْنَا * وَثَبِّتِ الأَقْدَامَ إِنْ لَاقَيْنَا
'O Allah! Were it not for You, we would not have been guided, nor given charity, nor offered prayer. Send down tranquility upon us, and make firm our feet when we encounter the enemy!' (Sahih al-Bukhari 4106)

Companions tied stones to their stomachs to suppress the pangs of severe hunger. Abu Talhah recounted that the companions showed the Prophet ﷺ the stones bound to their abdomens, only to discover that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had bound two stones over his own midsection due to even deeper starvation.

Witnessing the Prophet's extreme hunger, Jabir ibn Abdillah slipped away to his home and consulted his wife: 'I have seen the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a state of exhaustion I cannot bear; do we have any food?' She replied that they had only a small measure (sa') of barley and a young domestic goat (inaq). They butchered the goat and baked the barley flour. Jabir then went quietly to the Prophet ﷺ and whispered: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have prepared a little food; come with one or two companions.'

Bukhari 4102 says the Prophet called the people of the trench to Jabir's food and that they were a thousand. A figure of three hundred is not in 4101 or 4102. After they had eaten, the pot and the dough were still as they had been.

Bukhari 4101 reports a hard rock in the trench. The Prophet came down with a stone tied to his stomach, because they had not tasted food for three days, struck the rock, and it broke up into sand. That report does not describe three flashes or the keys of Syria, Persia, and Yemen.

A report from al-Bara' in Musnad Ahmad describes three strikes, and words about the keys of Syria, Persia, and Yemen. Edition numbers for that report differ. The number previously printed for it in this chapter is a different hadith in the edition that was opened, so it is not used, and no grade is assigned.

Bukhari 4101 stops at the rock breaking into sand. The three-strike report is a separate Musnad narration, and this chapter does not grade it or say that every later conquest was the fulfillment of that wording. What the companions did have in front of them was the trench, the hunger, and the meal that Bukhari records.

references.title: The Holy Quran
references.author: Surah Al-Ahzab (33:10–13)
references.notes: Description of the physical and psychological trials experienced by believers during the Trench.

references.title: Sahih al-Bukhari
references.author: Imam Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Bukhari (d. 256 AH)
references.notes: 4101 and 4102 are Jabir's meal; 4102 says a thousand ate. 4104 and 4106 are al-Bara' on the Prophet carrying earth and reciting the verses of Ibn Rawahah. 4105, on the east wind, is not part of this citation.

references.title: Musnad Ahmad
references.author: Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 241 AH)
references.source: Musnad Ahmad, report of al-Bara' ibn Azib on the trench; number not fixed
references.notes: The three-strike report is transmitted from al-Bara' in Musnad Ahmad. Hadith 18703 in the edition opened here is about prayer and ablution, not the boulder, and has been removed. No authenticity grade is stated.
